title: “A person intoxicated by craving Throws himself into the stream Like a spider into its own web. But the wise cut it off, Having abandoned…
content:
“A person intoxicated by craving
Throws himself into the stream
Like a spider into its own web.
But the wise cut it off,
Having abandoned all suffering, they wander on without desire.”

title: The nun Alavikā, knowing “That is Māra,” recited this verse: There is an escape in the world — I have realized it through wisdom. O…
content:
The nun Alavikā, knowing “That is Māra,” recited this verse:

There is an escape in the world —
I have realized it through wisdom.
O heedless relative (Māra),
How could you know that Dhamma?
Sensual desires are like swords and spears,
The aggregates are a chopping block.
What you call sensual pleasure,
I call no pleasure at all.

title: Elder Vaṅgīsa: Sensual desire burns me! My mind is on fire. Good indeed, Gotama — Out of compassion, speak The Dhamma that extinguishes the blaze.…
content:
Elder Vaṅgīsa:

Sensual desire burns me!
My mind is on fire.
Good indeed, Gotama —
Out of compassion, speak
The Dhamma that extinguishes the blaze.

It is because of distorted perception
That your mind is on fire.
Abandon the sign of the beautiful
That leads to sensual desire.

See formations as impermanent,
Suffering, not-self —
Extinguish great sensual desire —
Do not be burned again and again.
Develop the mind on foulness,
One-pointed, well-concentrated.
Practice mindfulness of the body,
Practice much disenchantment.

Practice the signless,
Destroy the underlying tendency to conceit.
By thoroughly penetrating conceit,
Your practice will be at peace.

title: “So too, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you might know health and see Nibbāna.…
content: “So too, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you might know health and see Nibbāna. And with the arising of the eye (of wisdom) in you, lust for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned, and you might think: ‘For a long time indeed I have been deceived, cheated, and fooled by this mind! For I clung to form, I clung to feeling, I clung to perception, I clung to formations, I clung to consciousness. Because of that clinging, there is becoming for me; because of becoming, birth; because of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”

title: “Monks, a woman, attending to her own female faculties, female deportment, female attire, female nature, female desires, female voice, female adornment — becomes lustful and…
content: “Monks, a woman, attending to her own female faculties, female deportment, female attire, female nature, female desires, female voice, female adornment — becomes lustful and delights in them. Through being lustful and delighting in them, she attends to external male faculties, male deportment, male attire, male nature, male desires, male voice, male adornment, and becomes lustful and delights in them. Through being lustful and delighting in them, she desires external bonding. With that bonding as condition, pleasure and joy arise, and she desires that pleasure and joy. Monks, through delighting in their own femininity, beings become bonded to men. Thus, monks, a woman does not escape her own femininity.”

title: “Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving there is for form — abandon it. Thus that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made…
content: “Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving there is for form — abandon it. Thus that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, so that it cannot arise again in the future. Regarding feeling … perception … formations … Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving there is for consciousness — abandon it. Thus that consciousness will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, so that it cannot arise again in the future.”

title: “‘Visible here and now, visible here and now (sanditthiko),’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is the Dhamma visible here and now,…
content: “‘Visible here and now, visible here and now (sanditthiko),’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise?” - “Here, Upavāna, having seen a form with the eye, a monk experiences the form but does not experience lust for the form, and there is no inner lust for forms. He knows: ‘There is no inner lust for forms in me.’ As long as, Upavāna, having seen a form with the eye, a monk experiences the form but does not experience lust for the form, and there is no inner lust for forms — he knows that — thus, Upavāna, the Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

title: Elder Hatthārohaputta: “This mind formerly wandered Wherever it wished, as it liked, as it pleased. Now I will restrain it thoroughly With wise reflection, As…
content:
Elder Hatthārohaputta:
“This mind formerly wandered
Wherever it wished, as it liked, as it pleased.
Now I will restrain it thoroughly
With wise reflection,
As a driver with a hook
Restrains a rutting elephant.”

title: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘washed clean’? He has washed away evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful…
content: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘washed clean’? He has washed away evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is ‘washed clean.’”

title: “Monks, just as a young man or woman, youthful, fond of adornment, would be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted if the carcass of a snake, a…
content: “Monks, just as a young man or woman, youthful, fond of adornment, would be distressed, ashamed, and disgusted if the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human were hung around their neck; so too, monks, that monk, examining the peril in those thoughts … the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”
